data.title: Palm Oil Ends Lower as Weakness in Soybean Oil Weigh — Market Talk
data.description: Palm oil futures closed sharply lower, weighed by weaker prices in Dalian vegetable oils and soybean oil, while concerns over elevated Malaysian inventories and slowing export demand added to selling pressure, says David Ng, a trader at Kuala Lumpur-based Iceberg X. Ng expects crude palm oil futures to find support at around 4,200 ringgit a ton and face resistance at 4,350 ringgit a ton. Market sentiment is likely to remain cautious amid weakness in competing vegetable oils. The Bursa Malaysia Derivatives contract for February delivery ended 54 ringgit lower at 4,332 ringgit a ton. (jiahui.huang@wsj.com; @ivy_jiahuihuang)

data.title: Pharmacy chain Big Caring ends 0.9% higher after $155 million Malaysia IPO
data.description:
By Rozanna Latiff and Yantoultra Ngui

Shares of Big Caring Group (BIGC.KL) closed 0.9% higher in their market debut on Thursday after the Malaysian pharmacy chain raised 637.8 million ringgit ($155 million) in an initial public offering.

  • Big Caring closed at 1.09 ringgit per share, above its IPO price of 1.08 ringgit, after trading between a low of 98 sen and a high of 1.19 ringgit. Malaysia's benchmark KLCI index closed 0.04% lower

  • The company sold 590.5 million new shares while existing shareholders sold 1.29 billion shares at 1.08 ringgit apiece, valuing Big Caring at about 8 billion ringgit

  • Nineteen cornerstone investors, which commit to purchasing shares before trading begins, took up 41.2% of the institutional offering. They included International Finance Corp, JPMorgan Asset Management (Singapore) and Eastspring Investments

  • Big Caring operates 668 pharmacy outlets in Malaysia under brands including BIG Pharmacy, CARiNG Pharmacy, Wellings Pharmacy, Georgetown Pharmacy, Ting Pharmacy and iCare Pharmacy

  • The company plans to use 89.5% of IPO proceeds, or 570.7 million ringgit, to repay bank borrowings and use 30 million ringgit to help fund a new distribution centre

  • Big Caring's net profit for the financial year ended June 30 surged 56.7% to 191.6 million ringgit, while revenue grew 17.9% to 4.02 billion ringgit, underpinned by store launches, higher sales at existing outlets and acquisitions

($1 = 4.1220 ringgit)

data.title: Moody's Ratings withdraws MUFG Securities (Europe) N.V.'s ratings following reorganization
data.description: Tokyo, November 19, 2026-- Moody's Ratings has withdrawn MUFG Securities N.V.' s A1 long-term issuer ratings because of reorganization. The withdrawal reflects the merger of MUSEU into MUFG Bank N.V. on 1 November 2026, with MBE as the surviving entity, as part of Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Inc.' s reorganization.

data.title: Lynch yacht crew unaware of wind risk before fatal sinking, UK report finds
data.description:
By Paul Sandle

The crew of British tech tycoon Mike Lynch's yacht, which sank off Sicily in 2024 killing him and six others, was unaware of its vulnerability to strong winds because the risk had never been assessed, a British investigation found on Thursday.

The 56-metre-long (184-foot) Bayesian was moored off Porticello, near Palermo, in August 2024 when it was hit by a violent downburst in a storm, forcing it onto its side, where it began taking on water.

Unable to right itself, the yacht flooded, capsized and sank around 18 minutes later, Britain's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) said.

Lynch, a British tech entrepreneur, had been celebrating his acquittal on 15 counts of fraud two months earlier over the sale of his company Autonomy to Hewlett Packard.

He was sailing with his family and friends who supported him during the US trial.

His 18-year-old daughter Hannah died, along with lawyer Chris Morvillo and his wife Neda, banker Jonathan Bloomer and his wife Judy, and chef Recaldo Thomas.

The yacht was vulnerable to violent winds and was probably knocked over by gusts of more than 117 kilometres (73 miles) per hour, British investigators said in 2025.

Thursday's report by the MAIB, which was not designed to determine liability, said the yacht's vulnerability to wind when operating under engine power had never been assessed, leaving its 10-person crew unaware of a critical risk.

Its 72-metre mast and furled sails contributed significantly to the risk, the report said. The yacht's stability information book did not identify its vulnerabilities when anchored with its sails furled and keel raised, meaning neither the owner nor crew knew of the danger.

"The vulnerability of Bayesian to wind heeling moments while in the motoring condition had never been assessed, resulting in the crew being unaware of a critical risk to the vessel and unable to take account of it in their operations," it said.

The report said the safety of the six guests and nine crew members who escaped the yacht and were rescued relied heavily on the training, experience and initiative of individual crew members.

The Bayesian was built in 2008 by Perini Navi, an Italian luxury yacht maker owned by the Italian Sea Group.

The company in 2024 said the sinking was due to a chain of human errors, and if the crew had shut all doors and hatches, turned on the engine, lifted the anchor, lowered the keel and turned the yacht to face the wind, it would have suffered no damage.

data.title: Stock rally keeps rupee upbeat, traders eye exporters for fresh fuel
data.description:
By Jaspreet Kalra

The Indian rupee strengthened on Thursday to touch its strongest level in seven months, boosted by an ongoing rally in Indian equities, while traders and analysts closely track signs of improved exporter participation in the FX market.

The rupee rose 0.16% from its previous close to end at 93.29 per dollar, helped along by an 1% rise in India's benchmark stock index the Nifty 50 .

The Nifty 50 has risen over 10% over November so far, fuelled by a rebound in foreign equity inflows into local stocks. This has also helped the rupee strengthen by about 1.8%, the best month-to-date performance in Asia.

The wave of foreign money coming into equity markets has also helped ease pressure on the central bank to support the rupee, allowing it to pare its dollar sales sharply after months of aggressive intervention.

Traders and analysts are now watching out for signs of a rise in exporter dollar conversions — alongside the momentum in portfolio inflows — to gauge how far the rupee's rally may run.

"A break below 93 for the pair would then prompt exporters to convert their USD holdings, which could create a large momentum move lower (on USD/INR)," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note.

For now, corporate activity appears to be divergent across lenders with some pointing to a pick up in exporter participation while others continue to observe elevated importer hedging while exporters remain largely on the sidelines.

"It seems that clients are also waiting and watching a bit but that could change quickly as well," an FX salesperson at a large foreign lender said.

Elsewhere, the dollar index was down 0.1% at 103.7 while Asian currencies were mixed.

Later in the day, the focus will be on the latest test for the AI trade as Claude chatbot maker Anthropic gets ready for its market debut.

data.title: Trump, Xi and Putin Convene First-Ever Summit as World Order Shifts — WSJ
data.description:
By Vera Bergengruen, Jonathan Cheng and Marianne LeVine

SHENZHEN, China — President Trump met with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in this southern Chinese city on Thursday, in an unprecedented show of unity among the stewards of the world's three largest nuclear arsenals.

The first-ever gathering of the American, Chinese and Russian leaders was a further sign of the end of a unipolar world order dominated by the U.S. — and suggested that what might replace it is a more uncertain, and unsettled, reality.

"We are really making history," Trump said as the three leaders opened the 90-minute meeting, sitting around a large, round wooden table under a towering Chinese landscape painting. "No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about them."

The three remain divided by their competing ambitions and sharply conflicting visions of what a new world order should look like.

Russia and the U.S. are bogged down in wars, while Beijing faces mounting economic problems and is deeply reluctant to take on the kind of global leadership role historically played by the U.S.

What the three leaders do share is a desire to be able to operate without constraints in their respective spheres.

Putin wants Washington to stay out of his way in Ukraine. Xi wants the U.S. to accept his claim that self-ruled Taiwan belongs to China. And Trump has made pushing Chinese and Russian influence out of the Western Hemisphere a central element of his so-called "Donroe Doctrine" to reassert U.S. dominance in the region.

There was little indication that progress could be made on the major issues they brought to the table: the wars in Ukraine and Iran and the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

But for the three men in the spotlight, just sitting down together was the point.

The three leaders met at Kylin Villa, a secluded government guesthouse at the foot of the hills of Shenzhen that has hosted China's political elite and foreign dignitaries.

Going into the meeting, Trump embraced the historic gathering to promote an image of himself as a global peacemaker alongside two autocrats whom he has long admired.

"All my life I read you'd never want to have Russia and China team up. That was like 101 in politics or in warfare," Trump said in a Fox News interview before the meeting. "They both like Trump. Now, what happens after me? That I can't tell you."

He left Washington with his party reeling from its midterm defeats, eager to use his final two years in office to cement his legacy on the world stage. "We have a chance to accomplish a lot," he said as he departed for Asia.

Trump headed first to a meeting of Southeast Asian leaders in Manila and then to Shenzhen for the annual APEC gathering of Asia-Pacific leaders, hosted this year by China.

When Trump landed Wednesday in Shenzhen, Xi welcomed him with the pomp Trump relishes, personally greeting him on the tarmac, a first by a Chinese president, and arranging a colorful military flyover — just as Trump did for Xi on his arrival in the U.S. in September.

Trump offered little indication of what he hoped to accomplish with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, beyond opening talks on nuclear arms control. U.S. officials played down any prospects of a breakthrough.

Trump acknowledged in the Fox News interview that reaching an agreement on reducing nuclear arsenals would be challenging.

"When they look at me and they say, 'OK we'll do it, but will you reduce your nuclear weapons by 2,000 weapons?'...It's a hard thing to do," Trump said. "For me, it's a hard thing. And it's probably hard for them to do also."

The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, or New START, the last treaty limiting Washington and Moscow's strategic nuclear arsenals, expired earlier this year. Trump has pushed for a broader agreement that would include China, whose rapid rise as a nuclear power brings new complications to any denuclearization effort.

Trump had also repeatedly floated the prospect that his trip to Asia would include a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who is building his own nuclear arsenal. By the time the trilateral meeting adjourned there was no sign that a Trump-Kim session would materialize.

For Putin, the gathering marked a remarkable diplomatic comeback nearly five years after his invasion of Ukraine made him an international pariah.

"He's my friend," Trump said after greeting Putin for a two-way meeting earlier in the day. "We knew each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this."

Trump later said he and Putin had a lengthy discussion on Ukraine, suggesting there had been progress without offering specifics. "I think things are happening," he said.

The Russian leader had first proposed a trilateral summit alongside the APEC meetings as a venue to discuss ending the Ukraine war.

In the end, Putin's place at the sit-down with the leaders of the world's two largest economies underscored the limits of Western efforts to isolate him.

"Our three nations are united not only by the status of victors in the Second World War but mainly by our responsibility for maintaining international peace," Putin said at the meeting.

Xi, while playing host, has in some ways been the reluctant party among the three. Beijing has long said that it doesn't belong in arms-control talks, saying its arsenal is dwarfed by those of Washington and Moscow.

But Xi benefits just by being there. The meeting places the Chinese leader on an equal footing, for the third time this year, with the U.S. president, while standing alongside a close partner in Putin over whom he holds an overwhelming advantage.

"What Xi gains from this trilateral meeting is the chance to look like the pivot player in international politics, convening this would-be 'G3' on Chinese soil and sitting alongside his closest partner on the world stage, Putin, to negotiate with a remarkably friendly American president," said Julian Gewirtz, a China-focused official in the Biden-era National Security Council.

As Trump met with Xi ahead of the trilateral, he framed his "very special relationship" with the Chinese leader as the cornerstone of U.S.-China stability.

"As long as you and I are in charge of things, we'll never have a problem," Trump said as he met with Xi. "We're never gonna have a problem."

Write to Vera Bergengruen at vera.bergengruen@wsj.com, Jonathan Cheng at Jonathan.Cheng@wsj.com and Marianne LeVine at marianne.levine@wsj.com
